title: ShinyHunters Says It Won't Leak FBI Data — But Can't Control What Happens Next
summary:
A hacking group that claims it stole a huge amount of private data from the FBI now says it will not publish the information. But the group also admits it can't guarantee the data won't leak anyway.

ShinyHunters says it took the data last Tuesday. The stolen information reportedly includes FBI officials' job assignments, home addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, and social security numbers — for what the group claims are thousands of employees. The group gave the FBI one week to remove or correct a May report that said ShinyHunters threatens victims' families and tries to release embarrassing images. That deadline is now almost up.

On Monday, a ShinyHunters representative told CBC News the group never planned to release the sensitive data. "We have never intended to nor have we ever planned to," the statement said. The group says its goal was to fight what it calls disinformation about its tactics, not to demand a ransom. ShinyHunters denied asking the FBI for money, though it acknowledged its "past operations" — where it has demanded ransoms from companies — could make people suspicious.

There's a catch. The group already shared a 5,000-line spreadsheet of stolen FBI data with some journalists. It says that sample is only a small piece of a much larger trove, possibly two to three terabytes. When CBC News asked whether it has done anything to stop that sample from spreading, the group said it "cannot guarantee" what happens next, because that is "out of our control" and some journalists "violated our trust."

Ian Lin, an ethical hacker at Toronto-based Packetlabs, says that's a real risk. He's seen researchers online claim they have the data too. "There's going to be people that are willing to pay a high price for this data," Lin told CBC News. The FBI has not publicly responded to the group's latest statement.
why_it_matters: This story shows how hard it is to undo a data breach: once information is copied and shared, no promise can pull it back, and the people exposed are federal employees who did nothing wrong. It also highlights how much sensitive personal data governments hold — making them attractive targets, and making the theft of identity documents a risk that outlives any single hack.

background_read: The FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation) is the main U.S. federal law-enforcement agency: it investigates federal crimes and also handles domestic intelligence, so its employees' personal files are unusually sensitive. ShinyHunters is a hacking crew that security researchers have linked to large data thefts from companies in recent years, often demanding payment to stay quiet — a tactic called extortion.

Governments have been hit before. In 2015, a breach at the U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM — the agency that keeps records on federal workers and job applicants) exposed background-check files on millions of people, one of the worst government data breaches in U.S. history. It showed that once records are copied and moved, they can never truly be recalled.

That is why security experts treat promises like ShinyHunters' with caution. Stolen Social Security numbers, birth dates and home addresses are among the most valuable data for identity theft, because criminals can use them to open accounts or claim benefits in someone else's name — and stolen files are often copied, resold, or reposted by people the original thief never controlled.

CBC News is the news division of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, Canada's public broadcaster, and Packetlabs is a cybersecurity company based in Toronto, Canada's largest city. Ian Lin, described as an ethical hacker — a security professional who studies attacks, sometimes with permission from the targets — says demand for this kind of data already exists.

perspectives.description: If the data is genuine, thousands of FBI employees may already have had home addresses, phone numbers and Social Security numbers exposed — the raw material for identity theft and harassment. ShinyHunters' promise not to publish is thin comfort when a sample has already circulated; the practical defence left is for affected people to freeze credit and watch for fraud.

Professionals like Ian Lin treat the group's statement with scepticism: extortion crews have a history of leaking data anyway, and once a file is copied it can be resold or reposted by anyone. The fact that other researchers online already claim to hold the data suggests control has effectively been lost, whatever the group says now.

This fits a long pattern of attacks on government and corporate databases, such as the 2015 breach of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, which exposed millions of federal records. Governments hold enormous amounts of personal data, and hacking crews often operate across borders where arrest is difficult — so the incentive to attack keeps growing even as defences improve.

The signals to watch are whether any portion of the trove appears online, whether the FBI publicly confirms the breach and notifies its employees, and whether lawmakers tighten rules on how agencies store personal data. The case may also change how journalists handle stolen data — taking a sample can disrupt a hacker's plan, but it can also spread the harm.
